newsitem.title: USA: Halliburton deal positions it for long-term.
newsitem.headline: Halliburton deal positions it for long-term.

text.p: Halliburton Co's decision to pay almost twice the market price for oil logging company NUMAR Corp may dilute earnings in the short term, but long-term it positions the company for growth, analysts say.
"I really believe that this will give Halliburton a major competitive advantage in bidding for business," said Philip Putnam of Brean, Murray & Co.
Halliburton said on Tuesday that it would buy NUMAR in a stock transaction valued at $360 million, or $39.62 per NUMAR share, compared with 20-3/4 at which the stock closed.
NUMAR has a magnetic resonance imaging logging tool that uses the same technology as medical MRI tools to chart fractures in rock that indicate the presence of oil and natural gas.

Putnam estimates that NUMAR technology is used in two percent, or 800, of the 40,000 wells drilled in 1996 and they estimate that NUMAR's gross annual revenues could grow to $100 milllion and net profit to $2.00 per share.
"This company was an abvious target, the only surprise is how quickly the acquisition came, not the price," Putnam said.
Putnam noted that Western Atlas Inc had been another potential bidder.

Halliburton's chief operating officer Dave Lesar said in a telephone interview that the company would honour contracts that make NUMAR's technology available to competitors, such as Western Atlas, but would review them when they expired.
"Although we obviusly would have liked to pay less, there will be a very minor earnings per share dilution for the remainder of 1997. It's short term pain that we have to bear," Lesar said.

Lesar noted that Schlumberger Ltd, the largest oilwell logging company had competing technology, but the NUMAR technology was better and gave Halliburton access to the rough offshore waters, where so much of the world's oil exploration is carried out.
"This is a tool which is much more robust, logs faster than Schlumberger's and gives more detail," Lesar said.
Putnam at Brean Murray concurs, saying NUMAR's technology is way ahead of Schlumberger's.
"This acquisition opens up whole new areas of business to Halliburton," he said.

NUMAR had a net loss of $1.1 million, or seven cents per share, in 1996, although the fourth quarter was in the black and in the first quarter of 1997, its net income was $923,000, or 11 cents per share.
Halliburton is ranked third in its industry sector, behind giant Schlumberger and Western Atlas. Net income was $107.6 million in 1996, or $0.85 per share.
The companies expect the acquisition to be completed in the third quarter of this year.
